# Texas Smoked Brisket

## Overview

Brisket is a tough cut of beef from the breast or lower chest of the cow. Low-and-slow smoking
transforms the collagen into gelatin, producing moist, tender meat with a dark bark on the outside.
Texas-style preparation relies on simple seasoning and long hours over indirect heat.

## Dry Rub

The classic Texas rub contains only coarse salt and coarsely ground black pepper in equal parts.
Some pitmasters add garlic powder or paprika. Avoid sugar rubs, which burn at high smoker temperatures.
Apply the rub generously at least one hour before smoking.

## Smoking Process

Preheat your offset smoker or kettle to 225 to 250 degrees Fahrenheit. Oak and post oak are the
traditional fuel choices for Texas brisket. Place the brisket fat-side up on the grate.
Maintain a consistent temperature throughout the cook. The stall typically occurs around 160 to 170
degrees internal temperature when evaporative cooling slows further temperature rise.

## Wrapping and Finishing

After the stall, many pitmasters wrap the brisket in butcher paper (the Texas crutch) to push
through the stall faster while preserving bark. Cook to an internal temperature of 203 to 205
degrees Fahrenheit for maximum tenderness. Total cook time ranges from 12 to 18 hours depending
on the size and weight of the brisket.

## Resting

Rest the cooked brisket wrapped in butcher paper inside a cooler for at least one to two hours.
This resting period allows the juices to redistribute through the meat fibers. Slice against the
grain when serving.
